### Round 1
There are no results yet, and scores stay hidden, so these picks rest on how the task works. A placement is safe when every footprint cell's lowest missing target layer equals the landing layer, which is the highest build column under the footprint. It is unsafe when it seals a missing cell or adds an extra one. The baseline already fits this: a per-column 1x1 stem can learn height and lowest-missing-layer features, and min/max pooling over the footprint can test whether they are equal. The likely limits are sample count under a fixed compute budget, how strong the per-column and per-candidate reasoning is, and global context for ordering and DONE. The 3 candidates are diverse because hidden scores mean no single change can be isolated: (1) the baseline with fewer PPO epochs, so it collects more samples; (2) a stronger column stem, a 2-layer candidate head with global context, and a longer horizon; (3) self-attention over columns for global reasoning. All stay under about 2x the baseline's compute.

### Round 2
Scores are hidden. Round 1 only shows that all three files trained without errors, so I can't tell which did best and this round rests on reasoning about the task. The starting head pools columns, but a placement's correctness depends on one layer, the one where the brick lands. There, the target must need every footprint cell and the build must lack them, with no needed cells sealed below. A head that pools each footprint within each layer, then takes a soft 'any layer' (log-sum-exp) across layers, can learn this directly. The cost is moderate (about 1.7 to 2 times the starting network) and it uses only 2D convolutions. Separately, the default recipe updates the policy only about 32 times. Smaller batches with 2 epochs give about 112 updates, which may help a small network. Since scores can't guide later rounds, I'm spreading bets: a layer-wise head, a recipe change only, and a layer-wise head with same-layer neighbour context plus the faster recipe.

### Round 3
No scores are visible, so all I can use is priors about the task and the fact that every file so far ran without errors. Three ideas look strongest. First, fewer PPO epochs, so the fixed compute buys more fresh designs. Second, a per-layer placement head, so the network can match a brick's landing layer against the target's missing cells. Third, more frequent updates (r2c2/r2c3 recipe). One thing r2c3's layer head cannot see is the layer below each cell, and that is what decides where a brick lands. It also cannot see the layer above, which is where overhangs show. Global context is still missing from the placement head. The trunk's receptive field is small (5x5 plus pooling), which may hurt ordering decisions across the board. This round spreads the bets. A: an improved layer head (neighbour-layer slices plus the column head). B: the proven r2c3 file with 1 PPO epoch, a pure test of sample count. C: the improved head plus global conditioning, a dilated trunk and a longer horizon.

### Round 4
No scores are visible, so I can only reason from priors and from which trials ran cleanly. All 9 trials trained without errors. Two ideas recur. On the network side, a per-layer head lines each brick's landing layer up with the missing target cells. Giving it the layers below and above makes support and overhangs local features, which suits a game where bricks drop and order matters. On the recipe side, fewer PPO epochs give more fresh designs under a fixed compute budget. Since 2-seed noise is large, this last round should combine the most plausible ideas instead of testing new ones. I propose: (1) the richest layer head (r3c1) with 1 PPO epoch, giving about 1.6 times its sample count; (2) the starting network with 1 epoch, a clean test of the sample-count idea at about 425k steps; (3) the light layer head (r3c2) plus the adjacent-layer inputs, keeping 1 epoch.
